Overall, our work provides new insight into how LLMs internally encode truthfulness, offering directions for more reliable and self-aware generative systems.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: Disentangling Deception and Hallucination Failures in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs by separating knowledge existence from behavior expression?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression to disentangle deception and hallucination failures in LLMs, and constructs a controlled environment for analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Representational separability analysis shows that knowledge existence is a dominant signal in distinguishing failure modes.
Sparse autoencoder reveals feature groupings associated with different behavioral cases, indicating a global split driven by knowledge existence.
Activation steering can induce bidirectional transitions between correct and deceptive behaviors, demonstrating causal control over behavior expression.
Hallucination cases are not reversible via activation steering, highlighting the distinction between knowledge absence and suppression.
Deception involves suppression of knowledge expression rather than knowledge removal, as verified through jailbreak probing.
papers.abstract: Failures in large language models (LLMs) are often analyzed from a behavioral perspective, where incorrect outputs in factual question answering are commonly associated with missing knowledge. In this work, focusing on entity-based factual queries, we suggest that such a view may conflate different failure mechanisms, and propose an internal, mechanism-oriented perspective that separates Knowledge Existence from Behavior Expression. Under this formulation, hallucination and deception correspond to two qualitatively different failure modes that may appear similar at the output level but differ in their underlying mechanisms. To study this distinction, we construct a controlled environment for entity-centric factual questions in which knowledge is preserved while behavioral expression is selectively altered, enabling systematic analysis of four behavioral cases. We analyze these failure modes through representation separability, sparse interpretability, and inference-time activation steering.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Human-like Social Compliance in Large Language Models: Unifying Sycophancy and Conformity through Signal Competition Dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the shared mechanism behind sycophancy and conformity in LLMs, and how does the interplay of signal competition and confidence govern compliance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework showing that sycophancy and conformity in LLMs arise from a shared compliance subspace where social signals override internal knowledge through deterministic competition.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM compliance is predictable via signal competition, revealing a systemic misalignment where social standards override epistemic standards, and proposes an Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for developing robust, truth-seeking agents.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy and conformity are behaviorally correlated across models, indicating a shared latent susceptibility.
Both behaviors originate from a convergent geometric manifold (compliance subspace) in the model's latent space, with high directional similarity in internal representations.
Compliance is a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary where the Social Emotional Signal overcomes the Information Calibration Signal (S > I).
The Confidence Margin provides an inertial barrier against social pressure, but it is permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity under intense signals.
Models exhibit distinct resistance profiles: InternLM3 shows a sharp phase transition, Qwen2.5 has high baseline susceptibility, and Llama-3.1 has a noisy, gradual transition.
papers.limitation:
static nature of the evaluation datasets and focus on standard transformer paradigms
generalizability to implicit or multi-modal social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
future_direction: Extending findings to implicit social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
Implementing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for epistemic self-regulation
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into decision-making frameworks has exposed significant vulnerabilities to social compliance, specifically sycophancy and conformity. However, a critical research gap exists regarding the fundamental mechanisms that enable external social cues to systematically override a model's internal parametric knowledge. This study introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework validated by assessing behavioral correlations across 15 LLMs and performing latent-space probing on three representative open-source models. The analysis demonstrates that sycophancy and conformity originate from a convergent geometric manifold, hereafter termed the compliance subspace, which is characterized by high directional similarity in internal representations. Furthermore, the transition to compliance is shown to be a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary, where the Social Emotional Signal effectively suppresses the Information Calibration Signal. Crucially, we identify a "Transparency-Truth Gap," revealing that while internal confidence provides an inertial barrier, it remains permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity against intense social pressure. By formalizing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework, this research provides a blueprint for transitioning from instructional adherence to robust epistemic integrity.

papers.title: Calibration Across Layers: Understanding Calibration Evolution in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does calibration evolve throughout the depth of transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that calibration is a distributed phenomenon across network layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers, and identifies a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream that can improve calibration metrics without harming accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network’s forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Calibration evolves across layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers where models become overconfident and then recalibrate.
A low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream is identified, and perturbing it improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without affecting accuracy.
The unembedding matrix's null space plays a role in calibration.
Calibration is a distributed phenomenon across the network depth, not just in the final projection.
papers.limitation:
The calibration direction identified in Phi-2 does not generalize effectively to Mistral or LLaMA-2.
The analysis is limited to zero-shot MCQA prompts and may not extend to in-context learning settings.
future_direction: Generalizing calibration directions using gradient-based approaches and verifying alignment with low-rank structures in the unembedding matrix.
Investigating model internals to identify neurons or components that contribute to confidence modulation.
Extending analysis to in-context learning settings and cross-model/dataset transferability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated inherent calibration capabilities, where predicted probabilities align well with correctness, despite prior findings that deep neural networks are often overconfident. Recent studies have linked this behavior to specific components in the final layer, such as entropy neurons and the unembedding matrix null space. In this work, we provide a complementary perspective by investigating how calibration evolves throughout the network depth. Analyzing multiple open-weight models on the MMLU benchmark, we uncover a distinct confidence correction phase in the upper/later layers, where model confidence is actively recalibrated after decision certainty has been reached. Furthermore, we identify a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream whose perturbation significantly improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without harming accuracy. Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution
papers.research_question: Does the suppression of parametric knowledge in the residual stream arise from the radial dilution of the signal's magnitude, or from an angular displacement induced by orthogonal interference?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs resolve in-context knowledge conflicts through orthogonal interference in the residual stream, rotating hidden states rather than diluting signal magnitude, challenging scalar confidence metrics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs resolve knowledge conflicts via orthogonal interference in the residual stream, simulating adoption without erasing internal knowledge, highlighting the need for vectorial monitoring over scalar metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Logit decay for correct tokens occurs under conflicting contexts, most pronounced in final layers.
Norm dynamics vary by architecture; Llama-3.1-8B shows dilution, but Qwen-3-4B and GLM-4-9B maintain stable norms.
Interference vectors are quasi-orthogonal to truth directions, supporting the orthogonal interference hypothesis.
Angular deviation correlates strongly with performance drop, indicating geometric rotation is the dominant mechanism.
Compliance is characterized by simulated adoption, where internal truth is bypassed, not erased.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming truth and context interact as linear vectors.
Dataset scope restricted to fact-based QA tasks (MMLU), may not generalize to other tasks.
Focus on final residual state before unembedding, not layer-wise evolution of interference vectors.
Sample size of three architectures may not capture behaviors of larger or MoE models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently prioritize conflicting in-context information over pre-existing parametric memory, a phenomenon often termed sycophancy or compliance. However, the mechanistic realization of this behavior remains obscure, specifically how the model resolves these knowledge conflicts through compliance, and whether this suppression arises from signal magnitude dilution or directional geometric alteration within the residual stream. To resolve this, we conducted a layer-wise geometric analysis across Qwen-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B, decomposing the residual stream updates induced by counter-factual contexts into radial (norm-based) and angular (cosine-based) components. Our empirical results reject the universality of the "Manifold Dilution" hypothesis, as two of the three architectures maintained stable residual norms despite exhibiting significant performance degradation on factual queries. Instead, we observed that compliance is consistently characterized by "Orthogonal Interference," where the conflicting context injects a steering vector that is quasi-orthogonal to the ground-truth direction, effectively rotating the hidden state representation. This suggests that models do not "unlearn" or suppress the magnitude of internal truths but rather employ a mechanism of geometric displacement to bypass the correct unembedding vector, effectively simulating adoption while preserving the original structural magnitude. These findings challenge scalar confidence metrics for detecting hallucinations and underscore the necessity of vectorial monitoring to distinguish between genuine knowledge integration and superficial in-context mimicry.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: When Modalities Conflict: How Unimodal Reasoning Uncertainty Governs Preference Dynamics in MLLMs
papers.research_question: How do multimodal large language models (MLLMs) resolve conflicts when different modalities provide contradictory information, and how does the model's confidence in unimodal reasoning influence this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that decomposes modality-following behavior in MLLMs into two core components: case-specific relative reasoning uncertainty and a model's stable inherent modality preference, and discovers a monotonic law governing this behavior.
papers.conclusion: The framework disentangles capability from preference in MLLM decision-making, revealing a robust law linking relative uncertainty to modality following and providing a mechanistic explanation for hesitation via internal layer oscillations.
papers.key_findings:
A model's probability of following a modality monotonically decreases as its relative reasoning uncertainty increases.
A model's inherent modality preference can be quantified as the 'balance point' on the relative uncertainty axis, disentangling it from unimodal capabilities.
In ambiguous regions near the balance point, models exhibit internal oscillations between modalities across layers, explaining external hesitation and averaged following behavior.
Traditional macro-level following ratios (TFR/VFR) are misleading as they conflate a model's unimodal capabilities with its inherent preference.
The relationship between relative uncertainty and modality following is a robust and general principle observed across multiple models and datasets.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must resolve conflicts when different modalities provide contradictory information, a process we term modality following. Prior work measured this behavior only with coarse dataset-level statistics, overlooking the influence of model's confidence in unimodal reasoning. In this paper, we introduce a new framework that decomposes modality following into two fundamental factors: relative reasoning uncertainty (the case-specific confidence gap between unimodal predictions) and inherent modality preference( a model's stable bias when uncertainties are balanced). To validate this framework, we construct a controllable dataset that systematically varies the reasoning difficulty of visual and textual inputs. Using entropy as a fine-grained uncertainty metric, we uncover a universal law: the probability of following a modality decreases monotonically as its relative uncertainty increases. At the relative difficulty level where the model tends to follow both modalities with comparable probability what we call the balance point, a practical indicator of the model's inherent preference. Unlike traditional macro-level ratios, this measure offers a more principled and less confounded way to characterize modality bias, disentangling it from unimodal capabilities and dataset artifacts. Further, by probing layer-wise predictions, we reveal the internal mechanism of oscillation: in ambiguous regions near the balance point, models vacillate between modalities across layers, explaining externally observed indecision. Together, these findings establish relative uncertainty and inherent preference as the two governing principles of modality following, offering both a quantitative framework and mechanistic insight into how MLLMs resolve conflicting information.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided Thought Space Exploration Leveraging LLM Intrinsic Reasoning
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities represented within LLMs’ internal activations, and how can these intrinsic abilities be effectively harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, a classifier-guided search framework that leverages linear separability of thoughtfulness in LLM activations to improve reasoning performance without human intervention.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe effectively leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through classifier-guided exploration, advancing understanding and enabling practical application without human intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Thoughtfulness is linearly separable in LLMs' activation space, with a simple linear classifier achieving over 80% performance.
Different LLMs encode thoughtfulness differently across representation types and layers.
The classifier's logit consistently assigns higher scores to correct, thoughtful responses regardless of length.
The ThoughtProbe framework outperforms baselines on multiple math reasoning benchmarks.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms single-branch selection and majority voting.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for segmenting intermediate thoughts may disrupt natural reasoning.
The gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Misalignment between training objectives (final outcomes) and guidance criteria (intermediate progress) may limit effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for tree node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Explore step-wise feedback or hierarchical evaluation to better align classifier training.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated to possess intrinsic reasoning capabilities that can emerge naturally when expanding the response space. However, the neural representation mechanisms underlying these intrinsic capabilities and approaches for their optimal utilization remain inadequately understood. In this work, we make the key discovery that a simple linear classifier can effectively detect intrinsic reasoning capabilities in LLMs' activation space, particularly within specific representation types and network layers. Based on this finding, we propose a classifier-guided search framework that strategically explore a tree-structured response space. In each node expansion, the classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by identifying and prioritizing more thoughtful reasoning directions for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We propose a branch-aggregation selection method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their thoughtfulness scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Response Uncertainty and Probe Modeling: Two Sides of the Same Coin in LLM Interpretability?
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance? Specifically, does a correlation exist, and what mechanisms underlie it?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates a strong negative correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, and provides a feature-attribution-based explanation showing that higher uncertainty corresponds to more dispersed important features, making probing harder.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between LLM response uncertainty and probe performance, with higher uncertainty linked to more dispersed important features, making probing harder. It also shows examples where low uncertainty corresponds to interpretable embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong negative correlation between response uncertainty and probe performance across multiple datasets and LLMs.
High response uncertainty is associated with a larger set of important features in the LLM's representations, which hinders probe performance.
The probe model and LLM generation rely on similar sets of features, as shown by feature removal experiments.
The correlation is robust to variations in generation temperature, sliding window parameters, and prompt templates.
Using response uncertainty, examples where LLM embeddings align with human knowledge (e.g., brand categories, time cycles) can be identified.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between probe weights and prompt embeddings is not well understood.
The correlation is only observed in instruction-tuned models, not base LLMs.
The encoding and decoding processes for concepts are not fully understood.
A unified interpretability framework is needed.
future_direction: Investigating the analogy between prompts and probes.
Studying parameter changes during instruction tuning.
Developing a unified interpretability framework.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques have shown promise in revealing how LLMs encode human-interpretable concepts, particularly when applied to curated datasets. However, the factors governing a dataset's suitability for effective probe training are not well-understood. This study hypothesizes that probe performance on such datasets reflects characteristics of both the LLM's generated responses and its internal feature space. Through quantitative analysis of probe performance and LLM response uncertainty across a series of tasks, we find a strong correlation: improved probe performance consistently corresponds to a reduction in response uncertainty, and vice versa. Subsequently, we delve deeper into this correlation through the lens of feature importance analysis. Our findings indicate that high LLM response variance is associated with a larger set of important features, which poses a greater challenge for probe models and often results in diminished performance. Moreover, leveraging the insights from response uncertainty analysis, we are able to identify concrete examples where LLM representations align with human knowledge across diverse domains, offering additional evidence of interpretable reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Enhancing Language Model Factuality via Activation-Based Confidence Calibration and Guided Decoding
papers.research_question: How can calibration techniques be effectively used to enhance the factuality of language models? This paper investigates activation-based confidence calibration and confidence-guided decoding.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ACTCAB, an activation-based calibration method that reduces expected calibration error by up to 39%, and CODEC, a confidence-guided decoding strategy that improves factuality on challenging QA datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.conclusion: ACTCAB improves calibration by leveraging internal activations, and CODEC uses these confidence scores to guide decoding, significantly improving factuality on challenging datasets like TruthfulQA.
papers.key_findings:
ACTCAB achieves superior calibration performance, reducing average ECE by 39% compared to the best baseline.
CODEC significantly improves factuality on TruthfulQA, increasing True.*Info. by 50% for Llama2-7b.
CODEC is robust across different training data sources and LMs, unlike intervention methods like ITI and RepE.
CODEC introduces a modest decoding speed reduction (less than 14% throughput decrease) while greatly improving factuality.
The ECE loss, which uses soft labels constructed via K-fold cross-validation, significantly improves calibration over binary loss.
papers.limitation:
ACTCAB and CODEC require access to the LM's activations, which may not be feasible for black-box models.
The methods are not explored on generation tasks involving longer forms, such as paragraphs.
Interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC remains challenging.
future_direction: Investigate longer responses in generation tasks to enhance LM trustworthiness in practical use.
Enhance interpretability of the confidence signals and decisions made by CODEC.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: Knowledge Localization: Mission Not Accomplished? Enter Query Localization!
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption hold for all facts? If not, what is a more realistic assumption?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Query Localization (QL) assumption, which includes query-KN mapping and dynamic KN selection, and introduces a Consistency-Aware KN modification method that improves knowledge editing performance.
papers.conclusion: The Query Localization assumption provides a more realistic framework for understanding knowledge storage and expression in LLMs than the Knowledge Localization assumption, and is validated by improved editing performance.
papers.key_findings:
Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) that violates the Knowledge Localization assumption is widespread in LLMs.
For KI, knowledge neurons are associated with specific queries rather than the fact itself (query-KN mapping).
The attention module plays a key role in selecting appropriate knowledge neurons for expression (dynamic KN selection).
The proposed Consistency-Aware KN modification method, based on the QL assumption, improves knowledge editing performance over baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
The work primarily focuses on factual knowledge, and it remains unclear whether the QL assumption applies to other types of knowledge.
The distinction between Consistent Knowledge (KC) and Inconsistent Knowledge (KI) might be related to the pre-training process.
future_direction: Exploring how to reconcile the QL assumption with other current theories.
Further utilizing the QL assumption to improve model editing methods.
Integrating the attention module more effectively to develop enhanced methods for dynamically editing knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store extensive factual knowledge, but the mechanisms behind how they store and express this knowledge remain unclear. The Knowledge Neuron (KN) thesis is a prominent theory for explaining these mechanisms. This theory is based on the Knowledge Localization (KL) assumption, which suggests that a fact can be localized to a few knowledge storage units, namely knowledge neurons. However, this assumption has two limitations: first, it may be too rigid regarding knowledge storage, and second, it neglects the role of the attention module in knowledge expression. In this paper, we first re-examine the KL assumption and demonstrate that its limitations do indeed exist. To address these, we then present two new findings, each targeting one of the limitations: one focusing on knowledge storage and the other on knowledge expression. We summarize these findings as \textbf{Query Localization} (QL) assumption and argue that the KL assumption can be viewed as a simplification of the QL assumption. Based on QL assumption, we further propose the Consistency-Aware KN modification method, which improves the performance of knowledge modification, further validating our new assumption. We conduct 39 sets of experiments, along with additional visualization experiments, to rigorously confirm our conclusions. Code is available at https://github.com/heng840/KnowledgeLocalization.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities.
